newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Trans Hex hopes for higher diamond prices.
newsitem.headline: Trans Hex hopes for higher diamond prices.

text.p: Western Cape-based Trans Hex Group Ltd is pinning its hopes on continued good demand for its high quality alluvial diamonds and higher prices from De Beers' Central Selling Organisation (CSO).

In its latest annual report, issued on Wednesday, Trans Hex said the market currently favoured its production but the entire industry was keen to see the finalisation of the long-awaited new agreement between the CSO, controlled by De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd, and Russia.
The two have for some time been at loggerheads about Russia selling its diamonds directly onto the market, but Russian officials said this week that a resolution could be in sight.
"It will inevitably occur in some form or another and the industry will then heave a heartfelt sigh of relief," Trans Hex said.
"If it is followed forthwith by a long-awaited and also long-delayed CSO price increase, it will further benefit Trans Hex."

The group, which last year listed its international exploration arm, Trans Hex International Ltd on the Toronto Stock Exchange, said its concerted diamond exploration efforts "should lead to the group becoming a significantly larger player in the world's diamond mining business within the next five years."
Trans Hex described the rough diamond market as a "gigantic elastic band, being pulled in opposite directions".
"At the high quality, bigger stone end of the spectrum, demand has been very strong and prices as high as they have been in several years."
This had been due to the fact that the CSO had shown "relative restraint" in selling such stones over the past year.
In addition, "uncertainty, turmoil, confusion and resulting bureaucratic inertia in Russia... led to vastly reduced sales from this source," the group said.
Supplies had also been affected by political turmoil in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (former Zaire) and Angola.
At the same time, the retail demand for larger polished diamonds had been greater than ever.
In the middle of the rough market - 0.25 to 1.50 carats selling at between $150 and $400 a carat - the market had remained unchanged.
"It is not so much that demand for these goods has been weak, but rather that there has been a 'gravitational pull' downwards, as prices of cheaper goods have plummeted," Trans Hex said.
"The market for stones worth about $150 per carat... has been and still is, in a virtual state of collapse.

"Again, this is not because of any particular lack of demand for the polished (stones), or any particular glut on the market of these goods, but simply as a result of the drastic price reductions resulting from Argyle's withdrawal from the CSO and the latter's reaction thereto."
Western Australian diamond producer Argyle last year pulled out of the CSO cartel to sell its smaller, lower quality diamonds independently in a bid to get higher prices.
